title: Writing "Bailen cha cha y guaguanco" on the plane
summary: Fellove doubted Americans danced Cuban rhythms, so Machito wrote a tune on the plane home, recorded on the Tico album.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay. I understand you met Fellove there and he accompanied you to the airport.
What happened at the airport there? I understand something happened there that prompted you to write a tune.

Well, he asked me if the Puerto Ricans and the Americans danced very good the guaguanco, el cha cha cha, mambo, all the music from Cuba, and I said yes. And said: "oh, come on Machito, maybe you lose the touch because you've been in the United States for so long that now you consider anybody you see turning, that he is dancing Cuban music." I said, no, no, no, no, really, you are just like San Tomas, that you have to see to believe. So, I say goodbye to the guy and I get my plane. You know the pressure, the pressure that create when you get into the plane, you know, everybody is scared, even the pilot, so I just grabbed a piece of paper and start to write a number. I say: "I told you, my friend, or you have to see to believe, like San Tomas." They dance guaguanco, cha cha cha, mambo and whatever we play.
Okay. Now, you recorded that tune for "The Sun Also Rises" album, on the Tico label. What did you call that tune?
"Pineiro tenia Razon", and it was that ..
No, no, no, no, "Bailen Cha Cha y Guaguanco."
Ah - Ha, because you are telling Fellove that the people here know how to dance the Cuban rhythms, right?
Would you say that conversations like that is what prompted you to write a lot of your tunes?
